outcomes: Read training and validation learning curves together
lessons: When a correct gradient still fails

learning-curve.name: Learning curve
learning-curve.definition: A plot of model performance against a stated measure of learning progress, such as update count or training-set size.
learning-curve.explanation: A training curve calls Neuron::loss on all supplied training examples at each epoch boundary. A validation curve calls the same unregularized mean-squared-error loss on held-out examples. Reading them together separates optimization trouble from generalization trouble: both remaining high suggests poor optimization or an inadequate model, while training improving as validation worsens suggests overfitting. Curves depend on the measurement interval and reduction convention. They are evidence from one run, not a guarantee about every random seed or dataset. In this chapter the horizontal axis is epoch count: each point follows a full pass over the fixed training set. Other learning curves vary training-set size instead; check the axis before comparing them.

minibatch.name: Minibatch
minibatch.definition: A subset of training examples used to estimate one optimizer step.
minibatch.explanation: Neuron::step receives one batch and averages the data-loss gradient over that batch, including a shorter final batch. A minibatch uses fewer examples than a full-batch step, reducing work per update and introducing variation because batches produce different estimates. One epoch is a complete pass through train_data and can contain several steps. This chapter uses fixed ordered chunks for a deterministic trace. Production stochastic training typically shuffles examples between epochs so order patterns do not bias consecutive updates.

regularization.name: Regularization
regularization.definition: A modification intended to favor models that transfer better to unseen data.
regularization.explanation: L2 regularization adds λ times weight squared to each minibatch training objective; the Rust argument l2 represents λ. Its derivative adds 2λw to the weight gradient, pulling large weights toward zero. The bias is unpenalized. Neuron::loss remains ordinary unregularized mean squared error on the explicitly supplied data, so training and validation curves stay comparable. The l2 value is a hyperparameter selected with validation evidence. A regularizer does not repair leakage, unrepresentative data, or an incorrectly defined target.

generalization.name: Generalization
generalization.definition: Useful performance on relevant examples that were not used to fit the model.
generalization.explanation: Training minimizes an empirical objective on observed samples, but the real aim is usually performance on future data from the intended setting. A validation or test split provides an estimate of this transfer under assumptions about how the samples were collected. Generalization is not simply low training loss, and a synthetic held-out result does not establish real-world reliability. Model capacity, data quantity, noise, regularization, and distribution shift all affect the gap.

checks: A reliable learning_rate lowers validation loss below 0.2
The learned weight is within 0.15 of two
L2 produces a smaller absolute weight than the unregularized run
A batch of four examples gives three optimizer steps per epoch
Invalid batch sizes and hyperparameters are rejected
limitations: Fixed ordered minibatches favor determinism over realistic shuffling
The small linear fixture cannot display every form of overfitting
Only constant learning rates and L2 regularization are implemented
